newsitem.title: USA: Mexico makes progress but still way to go - experts.
newsitem.headline: Mexico makes progress but still way to go - experts.

text.p: By Rich Miller, Economics Correspondent
Mexico's decision to repay its emergency loans from the United States is a victory for both countries, but that does not mean that all their troubles are behind them, analysts said on Wednesday.
While Mexico has made much progress in putting its finances in order since its 1994/95 currency crisis, it still has a way to go before reaching full economic health, they said.
"The economic situation in Mexico has improved strongly," said Nora Lustig, of the Brookings Institution think tank. "But the country has to continue to be careful."
Mexico took a big step on Wednesday to shed the stigma of the peso crisis by announcing it would pay off the remainder of a $12.5 billion emergency bailout from the U.S. Treasury.

President Bill Clinton hailed Mexico's action as a vindication of his decision to help the country out of its financial crisis two years ago despite criticism that he was bailing out Wall Street investors who had put their money there.

"Two years ago helping our friend and neighbour in a time of need was quite controversial," Clinton added. "Some said that we should not get involved, that the money would never be repaid, that Mexico should fend for itself. They were wrong."
U.S. officials though warned investors against expecting similar-style rescues in the future by Washington.
"The United States cannot and will not be any kind of global lender of last resort," U.S. Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers said.
Analysts though cautioned that Mexico needs to be careful to avoid digging itself into another financial hole similar to the one that necessitated the U.S.-led bailout in 1995.
At that time, Mexico's trade surplus ballooned because an overvalued exchange rate made its exports uncompetitive and helped encourage an import boom.
There are some fears that could happen again. In real terms, after adjusting for inflation, the peso has appreciated 15 to 20 percent from its lows struck after the crisis hit.
"If they let the real exchange rate appreciate much further, they'll be in trouble," said Gary Hufbauer, of the Institute for International Economics think tank.
Both he and Lustig said Mexico should prevent that from happening by building up its foreign currency reserves through the purchase of dollars and the sale of pesos.
Other analysts advocated cuts in Mexico's sky-high interest rates to helped prevent an overvaluation of the peso.

John Atkin, of the Institute of International Finance (IIF), blamed Mexico's recurrent trade problems not on the peso, but on its heavy dependence on imports of intermediate goods to assemble into the final products it then exports.
"The growth in exports is being fuelled by a growth in imports," he said.
Much of that activity takes place along the border with the United States, in the co-called maquiladora plants.
William Cline, who is also with the IIF group that represents banks and other financial institutions, pinpointed Mexico's low savings rate as something to be tackled.
The low savings rate means Mexico is spending too much on itself, buying imports and pushing up the trade deficit.
Cline though said Mexico's current account deficit now was "quite modest" and nowhere near the $30 billion level reached in 1994.
The country faces other economic problems, experts said. Its banking system is shaky, burdened by bad debts and confronted by a growing number of debtors who refuse to pay.

"The shock of the drastic reduction in the value in the peso and the extraordinarily high interest rates in the early part of 1995 had enormous consequences for Mexico's banking system," the Treasury's Summers said.
"At this point, the system still faces strains, but those strains are being worked through and Mexico's financial health is improving," he added.
Summers said Mexico also needed to ensure that the fruits of economic recovery -- growth is now up to four percent a year -- was spread throughout the population.

"There's a lot the government has to do to make sure all the kids go to school, to makes sure everybody gets adequate health care, to focus on employment in some of the poorer parts of Mexico," Summers said.
